clue.text: Unusual lift Ann gets on a holiday trip, from French painter

indicators.note: something unusual is out of the ordinary, so the letters of these two words are put into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
a tour is a trip taken on holiday

explanation.surface: Ann gets an unexpected lift on her holiday, courtesy of a French artist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusual' rearranges LIFT and ANN into FANTINL; A and TOUR complete the name of the French still-life painter Henri Fantin-Latour.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri Fantin-Latour was a nineteenth-century French artist known for flower paintings.

clue.text: "I never cared for —— much … It was the girls I liked." (David Bailey)

definitions.text: "I never cared for —— much … It was the girls I liked." (David Bailey)

parts.words: "I never cared for —— much … It was the girls I liked." (David Bailey)
parts.note: a quotation clue: the photographer David Bailey said he cared little for the clothes industry he photographed, only the models

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: David Bailey, the London photographer, made his name shooting for magazines like Vogue but claimed the clothes bored him.
explanation.definitionFit: Bailey worked in style photography, so the missing word is the clothes trade he was paid to shoot.

clue.text: See representatives

parts.note: the Holy See, the Vatican, sends ambassadors to foreign governments

explanation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like a verb, but it is the Holy See, the papal government.
explanation.definitionFit: Papal envoys accredited to foreign states act as diplomats for the Holy See.

clue.text: Dalmatian resort area opened up by Italians

definitions.text: Dalmatian resort area opened up by Italians

parts.words: Dalmatian resort area opened up by Italians
parts.note: the Dalmatian coast of the Adriatic was conquered and made a province by the ancient Romans, the Italians of their day

explanation.surface: A holiday coast in Croatia developed by Italian investors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dalmatian resort' suggests a modern beach holiday; the Italians are Romans, who made the region a province of their empire.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman province on the eastern Adriatic took in Dalmatia and was won by Rome's legions.

clue.text: Ely church converted to secondary school

indicators.note: a converted building is changed to a new use, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Ely's church has been turned into a school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'converted' rearranges ELY plus CE (Church of England); Ely is an English cathedral city.
explanation.definitionFit: In France a state secondary school for older pupils takes this name.

clue.text: One of Gustave Aimard's eponymous Arkansans

definitions.text: One of Gustave Aimard's eponymous Arkansans

parts.words: One of Gustave Aimard's eponymous Arkansans
parts.note: Aimard wrote a frontier novel whose title names the fur hunters of Arkansas

explanation.walkthrough: Gustave Aimard's adventure novel is 'Les Trappeurs de l'Arkansas'; its title characters give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Aimard's title figures are fur hunters who catch animals in snares in the Arkansas wilderness.

clue.text: Like those sweeter melodies?

parts.note: alludes to Keats's line that heard melodies are sweet, but those not heard are sweeter

explanation.walkthrough: From Keats's 'Ode on a Grecian Urn': 'Heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard / Are sweeter'.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats claims the music only imagined, never actually listened to, beats any real tune.

clue.text: Artist wins constituency?

parts.note: to win is to gain
a borough was a town sending its own member to Parliament

explanation.surface: A painter is elected to Parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Gainsborough was the English portrait and landscape painter; the question mark flags the political reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Gainsborough was an eighteenth-century English portrait and landscape painter.

clue.text: The -s of divine vengeance, if I may so describe the Bodleian Library" (A. E. Housman)

definitions.text: The -s of divine vengeance, if I may so describe the Bodleian Library" (A. E. Housman)

parts.words: The -s of divine vengeance, if I may so describe the Bodleian Library" (A. E. Housman)
parts.note: a quotation clue: Housman called the Oxford library a store of weapons for divine vengeance

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation from A. E. Housman; the dash marks the missing word, a store of weapons.
explanation.definitionFit: Housman pictures the library as a weapons store from which heavenly punishment is armed.

clue.text: Poet finds that anti-smoking movement sticks in the throat

indicators.note: the second piece is lodged inside the first, as something sticks inside a throat

parts.note: craw is an old word for the throat or crop
ASH is Action on Smoking and Health, a British anti-smoking charity

explanation.surface: A poet finds the campaign against cigarettes hard to swallow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anti-smoking movement' is Action on Smoking and Health, a UK charity; 'sticks in the throat' reads as an idiom for something hard to accept.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Crashaw was a seventeenth-century English metaphysical writer of religious verse.

clue.text: Seasonal restraint for German court painter

parts.note: winter is one of the seasons
a halter is a rope or strap restraining a horse

explanation.surface: A seasonal check on a painter at a German court.
explanation.walkthrough: Franz Xaver Winterhalter painted royal portraits for European courts, including Queen Victoria's.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Xaver Winterhalter was the German portraitist of nineteenth-century royalty.

clue.text: One Iris revised, making it louder

indicators.note: a revised text has been reworked, so these letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone revises Iris and makes her sound bolder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revised' rearranges ONE and IRIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that makes more noise is the comparative of noisy.

clue.text: Justify the formerly ill-favoured

parts.note: ex- means former
ill-favoured means unattractive, plain-looking

explanation.surface: Someone defends people who used to be ugly.
explanation.definitionFit: To account for something is to give reasons that make it clear and defensible.

clue.text: Deposits money for Sir Joseph, the botanist ()

explanation.surface: Sir Joseph the botanist puts money away.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Joseph Banks sailed with Captain Cook as botanist on the Endeavour.
explanation.definitionFit: One putting cash in an account lodges it; Sir Joseph Banks was the naturalist on Cook's first voyage.

clue.text: Poet bringing some high pressure to Fabian economist

parts.note: G. D. H. Cole was a socialist economist of the Fabian Society
a ridge is an elongated area of high atmospheric pressure

explanation.surface: A poet puts pressure on a socialist economist.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fabian Society is a British socialist think tank; a ridge is a weather-map term for a strip of high pressure.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Taylor Coleridge was the Romantic author of 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner'.

clue.text: Use of antiseptic techniques stirs Emil somehow

indicators.note: somehow suggests an uncertain arrangement, so these letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: Emil gets stirred up about hospital hygiene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges STIRS and EMIL; Joseph Lister pioneered antiseptic surgery.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Lister introduced carbolic acid sterilisation to surgery, and his method bears his name.

clue.text: Places to retire to for Homer's set, strangely enough

indicators.note: strangely signals the letters of these words are put in an odd new order

parts.note: the possessive S is kept as a letter here

explanation.surface: Homer's crowd, oddly, chooses retirement villages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strangely enough' rearranges HOMERS and SET; the possessive S counts as a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Elderly people move into residential care houses on retiring.

clue.text: Exposed ridge an obstruction to Chopin's friend?

parts.note: George Sand, the French novelist, was Chopin's lover
a bar blocks the way

explanation.surface: A ridge is something keeping Chopin's companion away.
explanation.walkthrough: George Sand was the pen name of the French novelist who lived with Chopin.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoal of sediment showing at low tide forms a ridge in the water.

clue.text: Article supporting pastime, say, of a follower of mechanistic political philosophy

definitions.text: of a follower of mechanistic political philosophy

indicators.note: in a down clue the article sits beneath, holding up the other piece
say signals the word for a pastime is taken as it sounds, spelt differently

parts.note: a hobby is a pastime
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: An article backing a hobby turns out to be about political philosophy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' gives HOBBI, the sound of HOBBY; 'supporting' puts AN below it. Thomas Hobbes argued in 'Leviathan' for a mechanistic view of man and state.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Hobbes's materialist theory of the state gives the adjective for his followers.

clue.text: Female poet gets a penny to strip ()

parts.note: a lath is a thin strip of wood

explanation.surface: A woman poet is paid a penny to undress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strip' reads as a verb but is a noun, a thin strip of wood. Sylvia Plath was the American poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Sylvia Plath was the American author of 'Ariel' and 'The Bell Jar'.

clue.text: Talented groups could be seen as palsied

indicators.note: signals the letters of the following word may be rearranged into another word

explanation.surface: Gifted ensembles might be thought to be shaky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be seen as' rearranges PALSIED; the Pléiade was a group of French Renaissance poets, and the word extends to any brilliant group of seven.
explanation.definitionFit: After the seven stars of the Pleiades, the word names a brilliant cluster of gifted people.

clue.text: "With a thousand Ta's and Pardon's / Daintily —— Elaine" (Betjeman)

definitions.text: "With a thousand Ta's and Pardon's / Daintily —— Elaine" (Betjeman)

parts.words: "With a thousand Ta's and Pardon's / Daintily —— Elaine" (Betjeman)
parts.note: a quotation clue: in Betjeman's poem Elaine steps down from a train

explanation.walkthrough: From Betjeman's 'Middlesex', where Elaine gets off the electric train at Ruislip Gardens, a London suburb.
explanation.definitionFit: Elaine gets down from the carriage, the verb for stepping off a vehicle.

clue.text: Dishonourable international group stands by old currency

parts.note: the UN is the United Nations
a noble was an old English gold coin

explanation.surface: The United Nations behaves dishonourably over old money.
explanation.walkthrough: The noble was a medieval English gold coin worth a third of a pound.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking honour, ignoble.

clue.text: Poems revised for old salts

indicators.note: revised poems are reworked, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Poems are rewritten about veteran sailors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old salts' looks like sailors, but means Epsom salts, magnesium sulphate, named after the Surrey town.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsom salts, magnesium sulphate, take the name of the Surrey spa town.

clue.text: Guest of Nebuchadnezzar with an eye to the future

definitions.text: Guest of Nebuchadnezzar with an eye to the future

parts.words: Guest of Nebuchadnezzar with an eye to the future
parts.note: a Hebrew prophet held among the exiles in Babylon

explanation.walkthrough: 'Guest' is ironic: the prophet was a deportee in Nebuchadnezzar's Babylon, and 'eye to the future' marks him as a prophet.
explanation.definitionFit: The Old Testament prophet lived among the Jewish exiles in Babylon and foretold events.

clue.text: Little creatures made from pieces on the cooker

indicators.note: the pieces are placed after the cooker word, sitting on it

parts.note: a hob is the top of a cooker
bits are pieces

explanation.surface: Small creatures are made from scraps left on the stove.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made from' is only a link; 'on' places the second piece after the first, as things sit on a stove.
explanation.definitionFit: Tolkien's small, furry-footed folk of the Shire.

clue.text: He figured in lists at Ashby de la Zouche

definitions.text: He figured in lists at Ashby de la Zouche

parts.words: He figured in lists at Ashby de la Zouche
parts.note: lists are a jousting ground; Scott's hero fights at the tournament at Ashby

explanation.walkthrough: 'lists' look like written lists but are the barriers of a jousting arena; Scott's novel has a famous tournament at Ashby-de-la-Zouch, a Leicestershire town.
explanation.definitionFit: Walter Scott's knight jousts in disguise at the Ashby tournament.

clue.text: Matriarch and patriarch produced primitive work

parts.note: a grandmother is a family's matriarch
Moses is an Old Testament patriarch

explanation.surface: Grandparents together produced some primitive work.
explanation.walkthrough: Grandma Moses was the American folk painter whose naive style is called primitive.
explanation.definitionFit: Anna Mary Robertson Moses was a self-taught American folk painter.
